title: Efficiency Ratio (ER)
summary: The net price move over N bars divided by the sum of every bar-to-bar move, from 0 for pure chop to 1 for a straight trend.
description:
The Efficiency Ratio (ER) compares how far price has travelled in a straight line with how far it moved in total. The net move is the absolute difference between the source now and N bars ago (10 by default). The total, or noise, is the sum of the absolute bar-to-bar changes over the same N bars. The ratio of the two lies between 0 and 1.

The noise total is kept running from the first bar, while the net move is zero until N bars exist, so the line starts at zero. A missing source value reads as zero, and the result is held between 0 and 1.
howToRead:
A reading near 1 means almost every bar moved in the same direction, so the market is trending efficiently. A reading near 0 means price went back and forth and ended near where it started, which is a choppy, range-bound market. The 0.5 line is a rough divider between the two.

It says nothing about direction, only about how clean the move was. Many traders use it to decide when a trend-following method is likely to work and when to stand aside.

settings.label: Source
settings.description: The price series the calculation reads, such as the close or the bar midpoint.

settings.label: Period
settings.description: How many bars the net move and the noise are measured over. A longer period gives a slower, steadier reading.

faq.q: Does a high reading mean price is rising?
faq.a: No. It means the move was efficient in either direction. A steady fall also reads close to 1.

faq.q: Why is it zero at the start?
faq.a: The net move is only measured once N bars exist, so until then the ratio is zero.

faq.q: Where is it used besides on its own?
faq.a: The same ratio is the building block of adaptive moving averages, which speed up when it is high and slow down when it is low.
